analysis.one_liner: Requires the largest banks to stop financing new fossil fuel projects and phase out fossil fuel lending by 2030.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee in March 2023 and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would force banks with $50 billion or more in assets to submit plans to the Federal Reserve to cut the emissions their lending and investing create — cutting them in half by 2030 and to zero by 2050. Within 60 days of becoming law, banks would have to stop financing new or expanded fossil fuel projects; thermal coal financing would end by 2025 and all fossil fuel financing by 2030. Plans could not rely on carbon offsets, banks would have to prioritize withdrawing from projects that harm low-income and minority communities, and banks that did not comply could face divestment orders or even loss of FDIC deposit insurance.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people, who bear the costs of climate change in disasters, health impacts, and insurance and energy prices. The bill also directs banks to prioritize pulling money from projects that disproportionately harm low-income and minority communities, and it requires the Federal Reserve to report on how to protect workers and communities affected by the shift away from fossil fuels.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyone exposed to climate change; low-income communities

how_it_helps.text: Covered banks — those with at least $50 billion in assets — must submit an emission reduction plan cutting financed emissions 50% by 2030 and to zero by 2050, and the Federal Reserve must reject plans that don't meet science-based targets without using carbon offsets.
Banks must discontinue financing new or expanded fossil fuel projects within 60 days of enactment, thermal coal by 2025, and all fossil fuel financing by 2030.

Banks must prioritize withdrawing funding from companies and projects with a disproportionately negative impact on low-income and minority communities, and support worker retraining and severance during the transition.

The Financial Stability Oversight Council would treat a company's contribution to the financial system's emissions as a factor in deciding whether it needs stricter oversight, and the Federal Reserve would report to Congress on the level of financed emissions, regulatory gaps, and options — including a public investment bank — for an equitable transition.
Banks that fail to submit or meet their plans face penalties including required divestiture of fossil assets and potential termination of FDIC deposit insurance.

analysis.who_pays: The largest banks, which would lose the fees and interest from fossil fuel lending and underwriting, and oil, gas, and coal companies, which would lose access to new bank financing for exploration, pipelines, and expansion. Some of those costs could be passed to energy consumers during the transition.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large banks and fossil fuel companies

drawbacks.text: The mandates are abrupt: a ban on new and expanded fossil fuel project financing within 60 days of enactment, and a thermal coal deadline of January 2025, would give banks and energy markets little time to adjust, and critics argue restricting credit could raise energy financing costs and prices while the transition is still underway.

The bill directs bank regulators to steer private lending decisions — deciding which industries banks may finance — which opponents consider beyond the traditional safety-and-soundness role of the Federal Reserve and FDIC, even though the bill frames emissions as a financial stability risk.

Coal-dependent regions could be hit hard on the bill's timeline; the bill responds by requiring transition benefits for affected workers and a Federal Reserve analysis of community impacts, but it provides no direct funding for those communities itself.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This is one of the most aggressive climate-finance proposals ever introduced: it forbids banks from using carbon offsets to paper over emissions and backs the mandate with real penalties, including loss of deposit insurance. The tradeoff is speed versus disruption — the 60-day ban on new fossil projects and the 2025 coal deadline give markets almost no adjustment time, and the bill relies on bank regulators rather than dedicated funding to protect workers and communities. It would likely be amended heavily if it ever advanced.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Banking Committee, which never scheduled a hearing or vote, and the bill died there when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Markey introduced the Fossil Free Finance Act on March 30, 2023, joined by Sen. Merkley and Sen. Sanders as original sponsors.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs on the day of introduction.
No further action appears in the record — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
The bill had five cosponsors, all Democrats or Independents, and no Republican support.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large banks and oil, gas, and coal companies came out ahead: they kept unrestricted access to bank financing for fossil fuel expansion, with no emission reduction plans, divestment orders, or penalties ever applied.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large banks and fossil fuel companies

sides.party_line_note: All six senators attached to the bill were Democrats or Independents — Markey, Merkley, Sanders, and three more cosponsors — and no Republican signed on.

industries.note: These banks collect substantial fees and interest from financing fossil fuel companies and projects. The bill would force them to cut that business on a fixed timeline, with penalties up to divestiture and loss of FDIC insurance — a direct hit to a revenue stream whose growth the public would be better off without.

They would lose bank financing for new or expanded wells, pipelines, terminals, and refineries within 60 days, and all fossil financing by 2030. Their business model depends on expanding extraction, which is what the bill is designed to stop.
Banks would have to eliminate financing for commodities whose production converts natural forest to farmland or plantations, cutting off capital for an industry that profits from deforestation.
Emission plans may not count carbon offsets, closing off a market built on paper reductions that climate advocates say often fails to deliver real emission cuts.
